Nobody tells you no. They just stop replying, and you file it as a no.

Go back to the day you sent the quote. You'd found the buyer, had the conversation and priced the job. Then you chased once, maybe twice, something urgent landed and the deal slid down the list. Three weeks later it had gone, and nobody could say exactly when.

Your buyer still had the problem. They solved it with someone who kept going. A second message, a third, a fourth, and they happened to be in front of the buyer the week the budget got signed off.

If you run a £2M+ business, that's one of the most expensive habits there is, because the hard work is already done. You didn't lose on merit. You lost in the third week of doing nothing.

Follow up is something you can build once and stop leaving to memory.

'Just checking in' isn't a follow up. Here's what one should sound like.

When we say chase every quote, most owners picture pestering people. A salesperson ringing round, asking if you've made a decision yet. Nobody wants to be that firm.

A proper chase sounds like you on a good day. A few days after the quote, the buyer gets a short personalised video, plus the extra detail they asked about on the call. A week later, a WhatsApp voice note in your voice. Two weeks on, a follow up that reads like it came from your own phone.

Every step is built around the buyer. Professional, useful, in your voice. And the important bit: it happens every single time, whether or not anyone remembers.

Buyers don't experience that as pressure. They experience it as a company that's properly organised.

Standing still never sends you an invoice. Not straight away, anyway.

Flat revenue feels safe: same turnover as last year, everyone still employed, a decent cash reserve and no drama.

So here's what a plateau costs. Say your firm turns over £3M. Growing 10% a year adds £300k in year one, and because it compounds, over three years the gap between growing and standing still is roughly £1.9M in revenue.

There's a quieter cost too. When you come to sell, buyers pay meaningfully more for a business that's visibly growing than one that's drifted sideways. That usually comes down to whether the sales side runs on a system or on someone's memory.

Standing still has a price. The invoice just arrives later.

There's one competitor whose name makes your jaw tighten. That feeling is useful.

It's telling you exactly where you're being out-operated, and it's almost never the product. Go back through the last three jobs they took off you.

A job you never heard about until it was finished? That's visibility. A customer of yours they nicked? That's follow up and staying in contact. A demo where they simply looked slicker? That's better education.

Every one of those points at something specific they run and you don't run yet. So write the losses down and build your own system properly, one thing at a time.

Give it 18 months and the positions can flip. They won't understand how you did it, because from the outside a good system just looks like luck.

The work rarely goes to the cheapest quote. It goes to the last one they heard from.

Plenty of firms that have been trading for 40 or 50 years still believe a serious customer will come back on their own. They rarely do, and it's not because they didn't like your quote.

They have a job too. Your quote is one of nine tabs open in their head. They get pulled into something else, someone goes on holiday, and a month later it's slipped through the net without anyone deciding against you.

When they finally sit down to sort it, whoever followed up most recently gets the deal. Not the cheapest, not even the best. Just the firm that's there when the decision happens.

The fix is a polite, professional chase in your tone of voice that keeps going until you get a yes or a no. We've spent 3+ years building exactly that for 40+ businesses, and it's generated £10M+ for our partners so far.

Enquiries rarely arrive at half ten on a Monday when everyone's sat there with a coffee. They turn up at the end of the day, over a bank holiday, or in the week you're away in Portugal. And that awkward hour is the one where a buyer forms his opinion of your firm.

That's no dig at your team. It's just how enquiries behave. If you've built a £2M+ business on doing things properly, it's an uncomfortable thought.

By the time most firms reply to a new enquiry, the buyer has already had two quotes.
